claims.claim: Honoré Blanc, working under French patronage from around 1778, produced some of the first firearms with interchangeable flintlock mechanisms and demonstrated muskets assembled from parts picked at random from a pile.
claims.episode_span: Early experiments at the French arsenals under Honoré Blanc demonstrated that lock plates could be milled to a common pattern and still function
claims.supporting_quote: Blanc demonstrated in front of a committee of scientists that his muskets could be fitted with flintlock mechanisms picked at random from a pile of parts.

claims.claim: Interchangeable manufacture rested on jigs to guide machine tools, fixtures to hold the workpiece, and gauges to check finished parts.
claims.episode_span: Gauges, often hardened steel plates or plugs, replaced subjective judgment with a binary test
claims.supporting_quote: Additional innovations included jigs for guiding the machine tools, fixtures for holding the workpiece in the proper position, and blocks and gauges to check the accuracy of the finished parts.

claims.claim: By the 1840s U.S. armories produced muskets with fully interchangeable machine-made parts: the Model 1842 was the first U.S. small arm so produced, manufactured at the Springfield and Harpers Ferry armories from 1842.
claims.episode_span: By the 1840s the Springfield Armory could turn out muskets whose parts were sufficiently uniform that a regiment could exchange components in the field
claims.supporting_quote: It was the first small arm produced in the U.S. with fully interchangeable (machine-made) parts. Approximately 275,000 Model 1842 muskets were manufactured at the Springfield and Harpers Ferry armories between 1842 and 1855.

claims.claim: The development of interchangeable manufacture took decades, spanning the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
claims.episode_span: full interchangeability took roughly fifty years from the first French experiments to routine American production
claims.supporting_quote: During the 18th and early-19th centuries, the idea of replacing these methods with a system of interchangeable manufacture gradually developed. The development took decades and involved many people.

claims.claim: Achieving interchangeability was a heavy up-front investment: for some years the firearms produced cost more to manufacture, and only by 1853 was there evidence that interchangeable parts led to savings.
claims.episode_span: decades were required to refine the gauges, to train inspectors, and to persuade suppliers to hold the same tolerances on forgings and castings
claims.supporting_quote: and for some years while trying to achieve interchangeability, the firearms produced cost more to manufacture

claims.claim: In a flintlock, the vertically acting sear acts on the tumbler, which is mounted on the same rotating shaft as the cock, holding the mechanism ready to fire.
claims.episode_span: each of which had to be filed until the sear engaged the tumbler notches at the correct angle and the mainspring delivered consistent force
claims.supporting_quote: The vertically acting sear acted on a piece called the tumbler, on the inside of the lock which was mounted on the same rotating shaft as the cock.
